I Don’t Browse, I Move In

Three years of reading, from a list in my notes

I keep a list of the books I finish in a notes file. It is not a sophisticated system. There are no dates, no ratings and no page counts, only titles under a year, sorted into whatever headings made sense that day.The list runs from January 2024 to {{updated}}: {{N}} books by {{nauth}} authors. Everything on this page comes from those titles and the year I filed them under.

If you had asked me, I would have said I read a bit of everything. I wanted to see if the list agreed.

Three shelves

Every book I finished, one spine each, shelved by year. Books by the same author stand together, largest group first, and a small gap separates one series from the next. Peter Heller is in orange.The count is the first thing to see: {{n24}} books in 2024, {{n25}} in 2025, and {{n26}} so far this year, which works out to a book every {{pace:.0f}} days.

The shape is the second. Look at 2025. I nearly doubled my reading that year, and I did it with {{a25}} authors. Sarah J. Maas alone accounts for ten spines. I didn’t read more widely. I found a world I liked and moved in.

Half the authors, most of the books

Oddly though, I would not have called myself a series reader. The list says otherwise. {{runs}} of the {{N}} books, {{runpct:.0f}} percent, were read as part of a run.A run is two or more books from the same series in the same year. The longest is eight straight books of Dungeon Crawler Carl.

{{th_years}} {{author_rows}}
Authors I read three or more times
Books

These {{nbig}} authors are half of everyone on the list, and they wrote {{bigbooks}} of the {{N}} books. The other {{nsingle}} authors got one book each.

One row is different. Every other name belongs to a single year, or two at most. Peter Heller is there in all three, never more than two books at a time. My guess is that it’s because his novels mostly stand alone. There is nothing to binge, so I keep coming back.

Fantasy is the base, thrillers are new

Fantasy and science fiction have been the base every year: {{f24}} of {{n24}}, then {{f25}} of {{n25}}, then {{f26}} of {{n26}}. What changed in 2026 is everything around them. In came {{thr}} thrillers, all of them Jack Carr and Brad Thor, along with a Japanese murder mystery from the 1940s.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Nonfiction makes up {{nf}} of the {{N}} books. Whatever I tell people I’m reading, this is what I finish.

Almost everything is new

Half of what I read was published in {{medpub:.0f}} or later, and {{recentpct:.0f}} percent of it since 2012. The typical book was {{medage:.0f}} years old when I got to it.

Two dots sit by themselves on the left: The Honjin Murders, from 1946, and A Wizard of Earthsea, from 1968. Both arrived this year.

What the list can’t say

A list of titles is a thin dataset. It can’t tell me when I read anything, how long a book took, or which ones I gave up on, and a 900-page fantasy counts the same as a slim paperback.

If I added one thing, it would be the date I finished each book. That single column would turn three shelves into a timeline.

Until then, the list says enough. I don’t browse. I find a door I like, and I stay until the series runs out.

Data from my reading list, last updated {{updated}}. The list has no publication years; those were added afterwards. Charts are hand-built SVG; the data and the script that draws them are in Data/books.
